title: Simply a Sign of the Season? Christmas Trees as Cultural Ciphers in Local Government Management of Diversity
authors: Gary J. Adler; Damon Mayrl; Eric Plutzer; Jonathan S. Coley; Rebecca Sager; Elise Wolff
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University; Colby College; Oklahoma State University; Loyola Marymount University
abstract: How do local governments symbolically manage the diversity of their residents? Drawing from an original representative sample of local government officials, we use a novel survey experiment with open-ended survey responses to examine preferences for cultural objects that symbolically manage religious diversity, an axis of difference that is increasingly salient to social conflict. Our experiment randomly varies the content of holiday displays on government property to measure diversity management strategies. Results show that government officials prefer the assimilationist strategy of a Christmas tree—by itself—over multiculturalist and exclusivist strategies, which both include sectarian religious content. Officials also evaluate Christmas trees as the content least likely to signal government endorsement of religion, compared to other holiday displays. We argue that these patterns can be explained by conceiving of a Christmas tree as a cultural cipher, a well-known cultural object that affords a range of meanings and resonates across social identities as innocuous. We argue that cultural ciphers are useful for an assimilationist approach to managing diversity because their ambiguity allows them to act as a vehicle of symbolic inclusion while also sustaining the meanings of majority groups. We also consider how cultural ciphers may lose their power for civic solidarity.

title: Incentivizing Equality? How Work-Family Policies Affect Parenthood Penalties in 27 Countries
affiliations: University of South Carolina, USA; University of Pennsylvania, USA
abstract: Work-family policies are theorized to shape the division of paid labor after parenthood, but recent studies have cast doubt on their importance. Leveraging harmonized longitudinal data spanning 27 countries and an analytic focus on couples and couple dynamics, our study shows that work-family policies do shape how divisions of paid labor change with parenthood, and that they also moderate the importance of couples’ relative resources as a determinant of the division of labor. We find that moderate-length paid maternal leave and greater childcare availability reduce parenthood penalties in couples’ division of paid work time, while prolonged leave exacerbates penalties. Furthermore, by focusing on couples, we provide novel evidence that partners’ relative resources do not operate uniformly across work-family policy contexts, showing that policies can incentivize couples to divide paid work in ways their relative resource profiles would not otherwise predict. We find that moderate-length paid leave and greater childcare availability encourage egalitarianism among male-breadwinner couples, although extended leave encourages greater gender traditionalism among female-breadwinner couples. These findings reveal that classic theories of household specialization and bargaining are not universal, and highlight the need for greater theoretical attention to how country- and couple-level forces interact to shape gender inequality.

title: Two-Sided Assortment Optimization: Adaptivity Gaps and Approximation Algorithms
authors: Omar El Housni; Ulysse Hennebelle; Alfredo Torrico
affiliations: School of Operations Research and Information Engineering, Cornell University, Ithaca, New York 14850; and Cornell Tech, Cornell University, New York, New York 10044; Daniel J. Epstein Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, USC Viterbi School of Engineering, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California 90089
abstract: On the Power of Adaptivity in Choice-Based Matching Platforms Online labor, lodging, and carpooling platforms decide not only whom users can choose but also when those options are shown. Simultaneity can crowd attention around a few popular users and leave many good matches unrealized. In the forthcoming Operations Research paper, “Two-Sided Assortment Optimization: Adaptivity Gaps and Approximation Algorithms,” the authors study how much platforms gain by updating assortments after observing earlier choices. They compare four policy classes, ranging from showing all assortments at once to fully adaptive policies that process users one by one. They prove that adaptivity within one side improves performance by at most a factor of [Formula: see text], whereas fully adaptive policies improve on one-sided adaptive policies by at most a factor of two; both bounds are tight. They also develop efficient approximation algorithms, extend their results to constrained settings, and empirically show that their methods perform far better than their worst-case guarantees.

title: Managing Newsvendors via Demand Shifting
affiliations: School of Data Science, Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen 518172, China; and School of Management and Economics, Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen 518172, China
abstract: How Demand Allocation Shapes Inventory Decisions Online platforms that fulfill orders for independent sellers often bear inventory costs without choosing how much sellers stock. In the paper “Managing Newsvendors via Demand Shifting,” Yilun Chen and Jiaqi Lu study how reallocating customer demand among substitutable products can influence sellers’ inventory decisions. The platform commits to a demand-shifting rule that effectively alters the demand distribution perceived by the sellers. Its optimal rule reduces demand fluctuations around a target inventory level, making that level attractive to sellers and pooling demand risk across them. The authors characterize this rule in closed form. When shifting demand is inexpensive, the platform can achieve the profit available under centralized inventory control, whereas sellers and customers also benefit. However, when shifting is costly and inventory is expensive for the platform, its optimal intervention can reduce customer service levels. The findings show why platforms should assess how demand allocation changes stocking incentives and customer outcomes.

title: Corporate Pension Risk-Taking in a Low Interest Rate Environment
authors: Vasso Ioannidou; Roberto Pinto; Zexi Wang
affiliations: Bayes Business School, City St George’s, University of London, London EC1Y 8TZ, United Kingdom; and Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR), London, United Kingdom; Luiss University, Viale Romania 32, Rome, 00197 Italy; and Lancaster University Management School, Lancaster LA1 4YX, United Kingdom; Lancaster University Management School, Lancaster LA1 4YX, United Kingdom; and Dishui Lake Advanced Finance Institute, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Shanghai 200433, China
abstract: We examine how funding deficit pressures shape the risk-taking of U.S. corporate defined-benefit pension plans and how targeted regulatory relief can mitigate these incentives. Using the 2012 Moving Ahead for Progress in the 21st Century Act reform, which temporarily eased funding pressure by revising discount rate calculations, we show that plans receiving greater relief significantly reduced their equity allocations and shifted toward safer assets. This derisking was most pronounced among active plans and those sponsored by more financially constrained firms. Our findings demonstrate that targeted regulatory relief can curb risk-taking incentives even without altering underlying economic conditions or financial reporting standards and shed light on the likely (and unlikely) frictions driving such behavior. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: R. Pinto acknowledges financial support from the Lancaster University Management School Pump Prime Program. title: The Equity Market Implications of the Retail Investment Boom
authors: Philippe van der Beck; Cameron Cohen; Coralie Jaunin
affiliations: Harvard Business School, Boston, Massachusetts 02163; Université de Lausanne, 1015 Lausanne, Switzerland; and cSwiss Finance Institute, 8006 Zürich, Switzerland
abstract: We quantify the equilibrium impact of retail traders on the U.S. equity market within a structural model of asset demand. Estimating investor-specific demand curves, we find that Robinhood traders are fundamentally distinct from all other investors, including other households: their demand is the most elastic and tilts most strongly toward volatile and microcap stocks. Each dollar invested through Robinhood generates more than five dollars in aggregate equity repricing, exceeding hedge funds, other households, and all other investor types. We decompose the cross-sectional variation in stock returns during Robinhood’s growth surge in 2020 into investor-specific components and find that shifts in Robinhood traders’ latent demand drove 11% of small-cap return volatility despite their negligible aggregate wealth share. To explain these demand shifts, we show that Robinhood traders are the only investor group whose latent demand is well explained by attention proxies: their demand exhibits a V-shaped response to past returns and rises sharply with trading volume. Our findings suggest that the growth of retail trading platforms represents a fundamental shift in the composition of equity demand with equilibrium consequences disproportionate to retail investors’ share of aggregate wealth. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Funding: P. van der Beck acknowledges financial support from the Swiss National Science Foundation. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.04854 .

title: Science-Industry Collaborations over the Business Cycle: Evidence from European Regions
“The Minimum Wage Is the Maximum Wage”: How Goal Replacement Perpetuates Means–Ends Decoupling
affiliations: Carl von Ossietzky University of Oldenburg
abstract: This research examines how organizations contribute to the perpetuation of means–ends decoupling (MED) within issue-based fields organized around societal problems, under conditions of heightened field scrutiny. In such settings, organizations often profess commitment to field goals and visibly comply with institutionally prescribed practices to satisfy monitoring, reporting, and public evaluation requirements. However, many adopted goals remain underachieved, raising questions about how compliance without progress endures and how claims of commitment remain credible under transparency regimes intended to spur substantive goal pursuit. Our data came from 75 interviews with 68 brands, suppliers, and third-party organizations pursuing worker well-being in global fashion supply chains. We unveil auditability-based goal replacement as an organizational-level mechanism through which actors rhetorically foreground compliance as public evidence of commitment while narrowing internal goal pursuit to auditable thresholds that serve their core goals, thereby allowing shortfalls to persist. Self-silencing about this substitution and the instrumentalizing of shortfalls close the configuration into a self-reinforcing loop. The study advances MED scholarship by (i) showing how organizations leverage field conditions and appropriate the existing scrutiny infrastructures to advance their core goals while reproducing the means–ends gap, (ii) problematizing the authenticity of commitment claims, and (iii) explaining how goal-ineffective compliance prevails as a credible substitute for adopted goals. It also extends research on organizational responses to institutional complexity and calls for greater attention to institutional impact—that is, the realized advancement of the societal aim an institution emerged to address.

title: Comparing Like With Like in Biological Invasion Risk Analysis
affiliations: Department of Ecology and Vertebrate Zoology Faculty of Biology and Environmental Protection University of Lodz Lodz Poland
abstract: ABSTRACT Biological invasion decision‐support methods are often compared under broad labels such as “risk assessment,” even when they perform different functions. This Perspective argues that functional commensurability must be established before methods are compared. In biological invasion risk analysis, screening serves an initial risk identification function, flagging extant or horizon non‐native species within a defined risk assessment area for prevention, surveillance, or more detailed evaluation. Comprehensive risk assessment examines entry or introduction, establishment, spread, and their ecological, economic, and socio‐cultural consequences in greater detail. Risk management integrates risk with feasibility, cost, effectiveness, legal constraints, and stakeholder values. Impact classification and post‐establishment population prioritization may contribute to these functions without being equivalent to them. Published comparisons show how conflating such functions can create false equivalence. The emerging Dispersal‐Origin‐Status‐Impact (DOSI) literature provides an illustrative example through its comparisons with applications of the globally implemented Invasiveness Screening Kit (ISK) decision‐support tools: population status and management priority are not the same quantities as prospective invasion risk screening, and species‐based screening does not imply coarse spatial resolution. Forty‐five peer‐reviewed ISK‐family studies report local or subnational screenings, including spatial resolutions comparable with or finer than DOSI applications. Valid comparisons require a shared decision objective, explicit spatial and temporal boundaries, independent evaluation evidence, and assessment of uncertainty and the consequences of error. These requirements permit methods to be evaluated for a common use, or combined within adaptive management, without treating disagreement between unlike outputs as evidence of superior performance.

title: Human Development and the Architecture of Everyday Worry: Latent Worry Profiles in the World Risk Poll
affiliations: Centre for Behavioural and Implementation Science Interventions (BISI), Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine National University of Singapore Singapore Singapore; Department of Sociology and Social Research University of Trento Trento Italy
abstract: ABSTRACT Whether public concern about risk rises or falls with national development has been debated for three decades, but the debate has compared countries hazard by hazard, asking how much people worry rather than how worry is organized. We provide a person‐centered analysis of everyday worry at global scale, applying latent class analysis to the six‐hazard worry battery of the Lloyd's Register Foundation World Risk Poll and linking profiles to the Human Development Index (HDI) in 140 countries (; 2023 wave), with the 2021 wave (; 119 countries) as an independent replication. Four worry profiles replicate almost exactly across waves, including a configurationally distinct secure‐basics profile (15% of respondents) combining low worry about food and water with high worry about crime, severe weather, and traffic. Profile prevalence is consistent with the ordered sequence predicted by a need‐priority account of worry allocation: pervasive worry falls from 33% to 13% between low‐ and very‐high‐HDI countries, low worry nearly doubles, and the secure‐basics profile holds steady across low‐ and medium‐HDI countries before declining at higher development. Traffic accidents are the most intense worry in every tier below very high HDI. These gradients persist after adjustment for self‐reported recent harm and demographic composition and are only partly accounted for by the objective hazard environment, though the cross‐sectional design cannot separate development from macroregional clustering. Development is associated with the composition of worry, not only its overall level; risk communication may be better matched to a country's worry architecture than to a single global template.

title: Toward Understanding Implications of AI‐Powered Intelligent Transportation Systems on Risk Research and Practice
authors: Shital Thekdi; Joost Santos; Unal Tatar; Samrat Chatterjee
affiliations: University of Richmond Richmond Virginia USA; Department of Engineering Management and Systems Engineering The George Washington University Washington District of Columbia USA; Department of Cybersecurity & AI Plus Institute University at Albany, SUNY Albany New York USA; Data Science and Machine Intelligence Group Pacific Northwest National Laboratory Richland Washington USA
abstract: ABSTRACT The rapidly evolving use of artificial intelligence (AI)‐powered intelligent transportation systems (ITS) and other emerging technologies in the transportation sector has the potential to deliver unprecedented improvements in safety and efficiency. However, recent research has also raised concerns about the implications of using AI and automation, as these technologies can introduce new, understudied risks to such systems. This perspective article evaluates AI‐powered ITS through three lenses: risk assessment, concerning whether current conceptual and methodological tools remain sufficient for these systems; the human element, relating to how analysts and operators interact with AI outputs, including explainable AI (XAI) and human‐in‐the‐loop oversight; and governance, concerning frameworks needed to manage these systems. Across these lenses, the article uses risk characterization as a diagnostic tool for locating where established risk practice must adapt and translates the resulting gaps into specific research directions. Although the practical interpretation and application of fundamental risk concepts may change when viewed through the lens of AI‐powered ITS, the work of this article provides a basis for research directions and requirements needed for risk practice to adapt to new and emerging technologies and to support future research and training within the risk analysis community. This perspective will be of interest to risk researchers, practitioners, and policymakers.

Navigating scarcity: sustainable supply network archetypes for water stress
authors: Ekaterina Yatskovskaya; Naoum Tsolakis; Jagjit Singh Srai
affiliations: IESEG School of Management – Campus de Paris , ,; Department of Engineering, Institute for Manufacturing, University of Cambridge , ,; Department of Supply Chain Management, School of Economics and Business Administration, International Hellenic University , ,
abstract: Purpose This study examines how firms configure sustainable supply networks (SNs) under water scarcity. It explains how water dependence shapes capability-configuration bundles and introduces transformational capability as the capacity to orchestrate capabilities for architecture-level redesign of SNs. Design/methodology/approach An abductive multiple-case study compares 13 multinational manufacturers across four sectors. Evidence from 23 interviews, site observations and secondary sources was analysed using Gioia-inspired coding and cross-case pattern matching. Findings Three contingent sustainable SN archetypes emerge: (1) “Stable”, (2) “Continuous Improvement”; and (3) “Progressive”. They differ in the scope of water dependence, the breadth of capabilities and the scope for reconfiguration. Static capabilities support routine monitoring and efficiency; dynamic capabilities renew existing processes and relationships; transformational capabilities orchestrate combinations of the five capability clusters to alter product and material choices, sourcing, governance, location, infrastructure or network structure. This is most evident in the “Progressive Sustainable SN” archetype. Research limitations/implications The qualitative study focuses on multinational manufacturers. Future research in other sectors, such as energy, should test the archetypes and transitions across smaller firms, services and other contexts of natural resource scarcity. Practical implications Managers can diagnose water dependence, distinguish incremental adaptation from transformational reconfiguration and align capability investments with changes across operations, sourcing, products, governance and network design. Social implications The developed framework can inform decisions on industrial location, catchment stewardship and shared water resilience. Originality/value The study advances a contingency-informed SN configuration perspective through a nested framework of sustainable SN archetypes. The archetypes are theorised as distinct configuration–capability combinations rather than as descriptive groupings of known adaptation practices. It establishes transformational capability as a distinct sustainable SN capability, rather than a synonym for dynamic capability, and explains when capabilities trigger architecture-level redesign under water scarcity.

title: The Many Faces of Process Complexity
authors: Sandro Franzoi; Thomas Grisold; Nicholas Berente; Jan vom Brocke
affiliations: University of Münster; Vienna University of Economics and Business; University of Notre Dame
abstract: Process complexity is a widely used concept for analyzing and improving socio-technical processes, but the term is applied in inconsistent ways, and its conceptualizations and operationalizations are often ambiguous. As a result, the same process can appear highly complex under one operationalization and comparatively simple under another, fragmenting insights across research streams. To map and structure the various approaches to process complexity, we conduct a scoping review across three domains in which process complexity has been studied: information systems, organization science, and computer science. We identify 21 distinct operationalizations of process complexity and organize them along six levels of analysis (process, between-sequence, sequence, partial pattern, action pair, and single action). By expressing these operationalizations in a unified notation and characterizing each by its underlying computation and level of analysis, we provide a means for measuring, relating, and comparing different forms of process complexity. This multi-level understanding allows researchers to investigate trade-offs, tipping points, and optimal degrees of complexity across processes. We conclude with a reflection on the implications for information systems research and practice.

title: Craft and Industrialization: Uncovering the Plasticity and Frontier of Craft
affiliations: Tampere University; University of Helsinki
abstract: Abstract Craft as an approach to work has been proposed as an alternative to industrial mass production. While industrialization has led to the replacement of craft logic with industrial logic to create uniformity and scale operations, the role of craft in industrialization remains ambiguous. Building on the analysis of engineering work performed at an R&D laboratory in the pulp and paper industry, we explore how and why craft enables industrialization. Our findings reveal how elements of craft manifest in engineering work by helping to transform ideas into useful objects, balancing scientific accuracy with practical usefulness, and fostering a sense of community and identity within the engineering field. These findings point to the plasticity of craft logic , suggesting that elements of craft can be transferred into new contexts and reinterpreted to address new objectives. Considering that these activities took place in an R&D laboratory that drove industrialization, they also reveal the existence of a craft frontier that escapes standardization by providing a context for crafting candidates for future standards. Craft frontier enables the coexistence of craft and industrial logics, where craft can contribute to industrialization by establishing foundations for managerial control without being absorbed into it.

title: Conceptual search: A generative view of entrepreneurial imagination
affiliations: Ross School of Business University of Michigan Ann Arbor Michigan USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Entrepreneurs cannot pursue ventures they never imagine. This article develops a generative view of entrepreneurial imagination as the construction of an evolving candidate set through generation, provisional evaluation, and revision. Conceptual search represents venture concepts as text, transforms them through interpretable operations, and compares their promise. A large language model prototype demonstrates complementary modes: local refinement lifts a concept from sixteenth to third among 30 ventures under a validated evaluator, while global recombination reaches distant possibilities that refinement makes competitive. The framework shows how search architecture determines what enters, survives, and develops, and how AI may broaden imagination within firms while producing correlated imagination across firms. By making imagination programmable, auditable, and experimentally tractable, conceptual search opens a research program on how entrepreneurial possibilities are constructed. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurs can pursue only the ventures they imagine, and valuable ideas routinely go unbuilt because nobody thinks of them. AI makes imagining cheap: it can draft, critique, and rewrite venture concepts in seconds, so developing ideas becomes a process that can be designed, run, and audited. I demonstrate a system that evolves real venture concepts: step‐by‐step refinement lifted a middling concept to third place among 30 real ventures, as ranked by an AI judge shown to predict fundraising, while recombining distant ideas created novel concepts that refinement made competitive. The entrepreneur's job shifts from generating a few ideas to governing many: choosing what to search, keep, and test in the market. One caution: rivals using the same AI will imagine similar ventures; advantage comes from proprietary problems, data, and evidence.

title:
Generative
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    use in entrepreneurship: An integrative review and the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework
authors: Jackson G. Lu; Gerui Gloria Zhao; Anna Manyi Zheng
affiliations: MIT Sloan School of Management Massachusetts Institute of Technology Cambridge Massachusetts USA; School of Economics and Management Tsinghua University Beijing China
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Despite the growing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in entrepreneurship, research on its impact remains fragmented. To address this limitation, we provide an integrative, entrepreneur‐centered review of how GenAI influences entrepreneurs at each stage of the entrepreneurial process: (1) opportunity recognition and ideation, (2) opportunity evaluation and commitment, (3) resource assembly and mobilization, and (4) venture launch and growth. Based on our review, we propose the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework, which not only catalogs GenAI's benefits and costs throughout the entrepreneurial process but also identifies potential trade‐offs underlying GenAI's double‐edged role. For example, GenAI may improve venture idea quality yet produce hallucinations and biases; boost entrepreneurial self‐efficacy yet heighten overconfidence; increase functional breadth and self‐sufficiency yet reduce prosociality; and enhance productivity yet diminish cognitive engagement, learning, and memory. We also identify features of GenAI that underlie these empowering and entrapping effects. Moreover, we explore boundary conditions that moderate GenAI's effects, including entrepreneurs' expertise, approaches to GenAI use, and personal traits and values. Beyond these theoretical contributions, our review and framework offer practical guidance for entrepreneurs seeking to use GenAI strategically while managing its risks. Managerial Summary We review how GenAI influences entrepreneurs at each stage of the entrepreneurial process: opportunity recognition and ideation, opportunity evaluation and commitment, resource assembly and mobilization, and venture launch and growth. Based on this review, we propose the Empowerment–Entrapment Framework to help entrepreneurs understand GenAI's trade‐offs at each stage. The future of entrepreneurship will depend less on whether entrepreneurs use GenAI than on how they use it. Used thoughtfully, GenAI may empower entrepreneurs by expanding their capabilities to engage in entrepreneurial activities. Used uncritically, GenAI may entrap entrepreneurs by restricting or eroding those capabilities. Entrepreneurs should therefore verify what GenAI produces, calibrate GenAI use to their expertise and task demands, and decide which tasks to delegate to GenAI while retaining human judgment for consequential decisions.

title: Beyond vintage rotation: bias-free sparse representation learning with oracle inference
authors: Chengyu Cui; Yunxiao Chen; Jing Ouyang; Gongjun Xu
affiliations: Department of Statistics, University of Michigan , Ann Arbor, MI ,; Department of Statistics, London School of Economics and Political Science , London ,; Faculty of Business and Economics, University of Hong Kong , , China
abstract: Abstract Learning low-dimensional latent representations is a central topic in statistics and machine learning, and rotation methods have long been used to obtain sparse and interpretable representations. Despite nearly a century of widespread use across many fields, rigorous guarantees for valid inference for the learned representation remain lacking. In this paper, we identify a surprisingly prevalent phenomenon that suggests a reason for this gap: for a broad class of vintage rotations, the resulting estimators exhibit a non-estimable bias. Because this bias is independent of the data, it fundamentally precludes the development of valid inferential procedures, including the construction of confidence intervals and hypothesis testing. To address this challenge, we propose a novel bias-free rotation method within a general representation learning framework based on latent variables. We establish an oracle inference property for the learned sparse representations: the estimators achieve the same asymptotic variance as in the ideal setting where the latent variables are observed. To bridge the gap between theory and computation, we develop an efficient computational framework and prove that its output estimators retain the same oracle property. Our results provide a rigorous inference procedure for the rotated estimators, yielding statistically valid and interpretable representation learning.

title: Salinization and Development,
affiliations: Technische Universität Braunschweig ,; CESifo and Technische Universität Braunschweig ,
abstract: Abstract Climate change-intensified seawater intrusion creates a dual shock of transitory freshwater shortages and lasting soil degradation. We study its impacts on agricultural production in the Vietnamese Mekong Delta, a major rice exporter. Combining river salinity observations and detailed canal network data to map localized hydrological shocks, we find that salinity reduces rice yields but generates disproportionately larger declines in output and revenue. These losses are driven by a contraction in land under cultivation and limited substitution toward salt-resistant crops, pointing to constrained short-run adaptation. Using household and firm data, we further document reductions in own-farm employment alongside minimal transition to non-agricultural sectors, suggesting frictions in labor adjustment. Beyond income effects predicted by Engel curves, households reallocate expenditures toward healthcare and children’s schooling. The increase in schooling spending is driven by higher participation and may reflect shifts in opportunity costs, though we cannot rule out forward-looking responses.

title: Sigmoid-Parameterized Lifepaths: A Dynamic Framework for Analyzing Research Trajectories in Scholarly Ecosystems
authors: Olha Buchel; Leila Hedayatifar; Selenay Aytac; Clara Y. Tran
affiliations: New England Complex Systems Institute; New England Complex Systems Institute, 125 Mount Auburn St., Box 380762, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA; Long Island University; Post Campus Library; 720 Northern Blvd, Brookville, NY 11548, USA; Stony Brook University; Stony Brook University Libraries; 100 Nicolls Rd, Stony Brook, NY 11794, USA
abstract: Abstract Traditional bibliometric methods cannot track dynamic research trajectories—they provide static snapshots (h-index), apply single-pass sigmoid fitting to entire datasets, or categorize discrete regimes, missing transitions and non-monotonic disruptions. We introduce sigmoidparameterized lifepaths: iteratively fitting sigmoid curves at regular intervals and plotting evolving parameters as trajectories through dynamic space. This identifies saturation dynamics—tracking entities' positions relative to ultimate capacity limits (acceleration, inflection, deceleration, deactivation), transition timing between saturation phases, and “time folds”—backward-moving saturation projections indicating downward capacity revisions from policy shocks or unsustainable growth recognition, and forward jumps indicating re-acceleration or capacity expansion. Bibliometric validation used carbon footprint research (2007-2023, 16,103 records, n=114 countries, n=7,960 authors): significant correspondence with independent regime classification (χ2=44.99, p<0.001), demonstrating convergent validity while revealing transitional saturation dynamics regime analysis cannot detect, country analysis showing saturation midpoints concentrated in 2015–2022, with backward capacity revisions showing a temporal concentration around the Paris Agreement ratification period consistent across window sizes and fitting designs, and forward jumps occurring at approximately one-sixth the rate of backward folds throughout the observation period, and author analysis revealing diverse career trajectories including sustained acceleration, premature saturation, and topic abandonment patterns that lifepaths capture through saturation dynamics unavailable in cumulative metrics.

Synthesizing Information-Driven Insider Trade Signals
authors: Jens Heckmann; Heiko Jacobs; Patrick Schwarz
affiliations: University of Duisburg-Essen; University of Liège HEC Liège
abstract: Abstract We propose a novel approach to synthesize presumably information-driven insider trading signals for the cross section of stocks. We find that the resulting straightforward composite strategy can often forecast returns in a global sample. This predictability is strongest in equal-weighted portfolios, short holding periods, and insider-buying signals, and it improves further with global diversification. Cross-country analysis reveals that varying insider trading restrictions between countries have limited explanatory power for the performance of the composite strategy. Overall, the results are consistent with a short-term informational advantage of insiders, which might be due to the skillful interpretation of non-private news.

title: The Weight of Compliance: Anti-Money Laundering Enforcement, Banking Sector Composition, and Lending
authors: Şenay Ağca; Pablo Slutzky; Stefan Zeume
affiliations: George Washington University School of Business; Temple University Fox School of Business; University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign Gies College of Business
abstract: Abstract We examine how strengthened anti-money laundering (AML) enforcement affects the U.S. banking sector. Heightened enforcement disproportionately raises compliance costs for small banks, especially in counties more exposed to money laundering. In these areas, small banks contract while large banks expand, increasing standardized, government-supported, and secured lending. While aggregate county-level credit does not decline differentially, local outcomes improve. Small establishments grow, non-tradable employment and wages rise, and real estate prices increase. The evidence is consistent with a reallocation mechanism in which AML enforcement shifts activity toward large banks, potentially improving intermediation quality through changes in the composition of local financial intermediation.

title: The Tipping Point: Interest Rates and Financial Stability
abstract: Abstract This paper studies the impact of interest rates on bank stability in a standard bank‐run model. Banks invest in long‐term assets, whose value decreases with interest rates, and set deposit rates to optimally insure depositors' liquidity risk. Liquidity‐risk insurance implies banks earn interest margins, which increase with interest rates. Hence, interest rates have two countervailing effects: they reduce the value of banks' long‐term assets while widening their margins. First, the paper characterizes the parametric condition under which an effect dominates. The condition implies interest‐rate risk is captured by banks' maturity mismatch adjusted for deposits' effective duration. Second, the paper solves for the interest‐rate level that tips banks into instability. Quantification points to the possibility of a negative effective maturity mismatch, making the tipping point a lower bound on interest rates.

title: Do Tax Incentives Enhance Entrepreneurship? Evidence from Value‐Added Tax Reform in China
abstract: Abstract This paper investigates the causal effect of tax incentives on entrepreneurship. Using a staggered Value‐Added Tax (VAT) reform in China as an exogenous shock to conduct difference‐in‐differences estimation, we find that tax cuts have a considerable positive effect on local entrepreneurship. A plausible mechanism driving our findings is the ease of financial constraints. Our results are robust to a battery of endogeneity and robustness tests. We find that regions with high levels of institutional quality, trust, or a commercial culture undergo greater entrepreneurship after the VAT reform. Overall, this study provides a timely policy evaluation of the importance of tax incentives in promoting entrepreneurship in a typical emerging market.

title:
Do
                    <scp>PCAOB</scp>
                    Inspection Deficiencies Related to Management Review Controls Affect Financial Reporting Decisions? Evidence From Goodwill Impairments
authors: Kenneth L. Bills; Chris E. Hogan; Jennifer E. Puccia
affiliations: Michigan State University East Lansing Michigan USA; Texas A&M University College Station Texas USA
abstract: ABSTRACT We examine whether PCAOB inspection deficiencies related to management review controls (MRCs) affect financial reporting decisions. Using the goodwill impairment setting, we find that firms are more likely to record goodwill impairments when their auditors have received more PCAOB inspection deficiencies related to goodwill MRCs. The association is stronger when inspection deficiencies are more likely to lead to changes to the design or implementation of an internal control (repeat deficiencies and deficiencies related to MRC precision). We observe some evidence that MRC inspection deficiencies increase the likelihood of goodwill impairment even when unrelated to goodwill, indicating that improving the audit of MRCs can broadly affect financial reporting. Our findings provide evidence that PCAOB inspections affect not only auditor behavior but also the financial reporting behavior of audit clients. Specifically, inspection feedback appears to influence reporting outcomes through changes in the audit and evaluation of MRCs, identifying a channel through which regulatory oversight affects issuers. The results have implications for audit firms seeking to remediate inspection deficiencies, for management and audit committees responsible for overseeing significant estimates and impairment analyses, and for regulators evaluating the broader effectiveness of the PCAOB inspection process.

title: When Politics Enters the Waiting Room: Far-Right Electoral Victories Exacerbate Discrimination in Access to Healthcare
authors: MERLIN SCHAEFFER; ALESSIO ROMARRI; DINA ROSENBERG; KRZYSZTOF KRAKOWSKI
affiliations: University of Copenhagen; Autonomous University of Barcelona; Rowan University; Collegio Carlo Alberto
abstract: Abstract Far-right political shifts have been linked to increased racism, raising concerns about their impact on minority access to public services. This study investigates whether far-right electoral victories encourage discrimination by street-level bureaucrats, who are expected to act impartially. We conducted a nested research design in Italy, combining a field-experimental audit with a regression discontinuity design focused on municipalities near the electoral threshold for far-right mayors. Research assistants with native-Italian and West-African accents contacted municipal healthcare offices to request registration with a general medical practitioner. Compared to native-Italian callers, those with West-African accents faced significantly higher rates of scrutiny and dismissive responses. Leveraging close elections, we find that this disparity was exacerbated in municipalities where far-right candidates narrowly won. These findings demonstrate that far-right electoral success can undermine impartiality and equal access to essential services.

title: The threat‐enhancing effect of authoritarian power sharing
affiliations: Associate Professor, Department of Political Science Emory University Atlanta Georgia USA
abstract: Abstract Power‐sharing deals can potentially solve the autocrat's commitment problem, yet often fail to prevent conflict. This article develops a dynamic model to examine a largely overlooked friction: Sharing power within an authoritarian regime bolsters the opposition's coercive capabilities. The resultant threat‐enhancing effect creates two distinct commitment problems for the opposition, which determine if and when power sharing occurs. First, the opposition cannot commit to refrain from leveraging its enhanced threat. The ruler prefers to incur a revolt than peacefully share power if the threat‐enhancing effect is large. Second, the threat‐enhancing effect tempts the opposition to wait for a future power‐sharing deal, which undercuts the opposition's commitment to revolt today. New dynamic implications arise: delayed power sharing, conflict, or an increased willingness for the ruler to share power are all possible. Scrutinizing the opposition's limited commitment ability contrasts with the predominant existing focus on the autocrat's commitment problem.

title: Geoengineering, Moral Hazard, and Disrespect
affiliations: University of Reading
abstract: Abstract Scientists and policy makers are increasingly exploring solar geoengineering as a tool for combatting anthropogenic climate change. Yet these technologies have drawn intense ethical criticism. One of the most influential critiques – the ‘moral hazard’ objection – holds that pursuing solar geoengineering risks undercutting mitigation efforts; and that, as a result, governments should halt the development of solar geoengineering. This paper argues that the moral hazard objection faces a dilemma: either the proposed solution to the moral hazard effect (that is, stifling geoengineering) is unnecessary, or it expresses a morally troubling form of disrespect. Articulating this dilemma serves three purposes. It shows, first, that the moral hazard objection is substantially more difficult to vindicate than it initially appears. Second, it clarifies what would need to be shown, empirically, to overcome this ethical hurdle. Finally, and crucially, it sheds light, more broadly, on what it means to respect people’s agency when designing and implementing public policies.

title: Beyond the Battlefield: Localized Civilian Clashes and Political Attitudes in Violent Conflict
authors: Carly Wayne; Sivan Hirsch-Hoefler; Masanori Kikuchi; Daphna Canetti
affiliations: Washington University in St Louis; Reichman University; University of Haifa
abstract: Abstract In protracted conflicts, civilians frequently encounter low-level, hostile actions from adversary civilians in nearby communities, yet the political consequences of these events remain understudied. We investigate this question in the Israeli–Palestinian context, examining how community-level exposure to hostile actions by Israeli settlers shapes Palestinian political attitudes in the West Bank. Leveraging a novel data set containing thousands of geo-coded conflict events from 2010 to 2020 paired with forty-six Palestinian public opinion polls in the West Bank, we find that district-level increases in settler hostilities are significantly associated with heightened political militancy among local Palestinians, associations that are larger and more robust than those from local Israeli military actions. A second empirical strategy examining changes in Palestinian attitudes before and after the establishment of nearby settler outposts reveals that this form of civilian land expropriation likewise leads to modest increases in political militancy among Palestinians in proximate towns. These findings highlight the distinct political impact of localized, low-level civilian actions and territorial expropriation—central but often overlooked features of sectarian territorial conflicts—offering insights for territorial and ethnic disputes globally.
